newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK SHARES CRASH, BULL KNOCKED OUT IN SELLOFF.
newsitem.headline: GREEK SHARES CRASH, BULL KNOCKED OUT IN SELLOFF.

text.p: The Athens bourse plunged 7.45 percent on Monday, a record fall for a single day, in a panic across-the-board sell-off sparked by a myriad of concerns.
Monday's fall means that in the past three sessions 1.2 trillion drachmas have been wiped off market capitalisation.

Stunned brokers debated whether it was the erupting Albanian crisis, a capital market commission warning which many claim pulled the rug from under a euphoric market or simply valuation physics pointing to a looming correction.
After powerful bull run early this year, certainly, hefty profits were there to be taken.

At the closing bell brokers weren't sure what had hit them. The panic selloff brought the share index back to 1,206 points, down 17 percent in three sessions with the previous raging bulls nowhere in sight.
"I was giving sell orders to hit any bid," a fund manager who wished to stay anonymous told Reuters.
In an avalanche of selling, investors pounded down even the very blue chips they were previously buying in frenzy. Bids disappeared fueling panic.
What went wrong so fast to reverse the bullish sentiment? Greece's brighter macroeconomic fundamentals had not changed.

CPI-inflation, down to 6.8 percent in January, was driving interest rates lower, making asset reallocation into equities a hot topic. The stock market which started the year with a bull run had gained more than 36 percent and still looked pumped up.

"I am not convinced it was jitters on Albania. It's just an excuse. The country is neither a military danger nor a great trading partner. I think retail investors just wanted out," said analyst Yannis Protopapadakis at ING Barings.

Many claim it started Wednesday after the capital market commission warned against rumour-based investment decisions, fearing speculation. The statement spooked players and many started running for the exit sign.

"The Albania factor is just another excuse. Commissioner Thomadakis did the great damage. Without his statement we would have had a normal, orderly correction and not everybody running for the door," said a portfolio strategist.
The ill-conceived statement, he commented, undermined market sentiment especially with retail investors. In turn, funds sensing a reversal also decided to opt out.
Other fund managers pointed out that the intervention to calm the overheating market could have been more subtle. State bank portfolios could have increased the supply of stock to contain the rise.

"I was expecting the market to stabilise around 1,200 points but I think this will happen around 1,120-1,150 points which is a 50 percent retracement. We'll see buyers come out there," said broker Alexander Moraitakis at Nuntius Securities.
In his view the Albanian flare up was not a serious reason and commissioner Thomadakis' statement was an excuse.

"Share prices had risen too much. We had a violent correction, an overeaction in the market. No one person can say something that can force the bourse to lose 17 percent in three days. No one is more powerful than the market itself," he said.
When Merrill Lynch analyst Mike Harris said Greek shares had limited upside potential, feeling the market was getting ahead of itself, the bulls kept on buying, bidding stocks higher.
"Greece was turning into a good three to five year story but the market was taking off too fast and getting ahead of itself," he told Reuters on Friday.

The deterioration in market sentiment might affect government plans to float another chunk of state telecom OTE and an initial public offering in the Public Petroleum Corporation (DEP) this year but psychology changes, analysts said.

"The higher the diving board, the bigger the splash. But really, if Greece was suddenly in war with Turkey how far down would the market have fallen? I see hype and overeaction, calmer days will return soon," said a private banker. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
